name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Deliver: Keep the Designs tab pure: designs only, live previews, taste-ranked

name: Reel
text: We need to prioritize manual review of design submissions to ensure quality and relevance, as automated filters may miss crucial contextual details. This approach allows us to maintain a high standard for the Designs tab, even if it means investing more time and effort upfront. By choosing manual review, we're accepting the trade-off of increased labor costs, but this is necessary to guarantee the purity and taste-ranked nature of the designs. This decision will enable the bus task to complete efficiently, as it will receive a curated and reliable set of designs.

name: Scriv
text: Manual review is a bottleneck—it slows down every submission and shifts the SLA burden to Marketing, who now own both the queue and the delays. Instead, let the submitter self-select quality upfront with a lightweight, low-friction triage step (e.g., "Does this meet basic taste criteria?"). Settle it by running a 2-week A/B test: one bucket with manual review, one with self-triage, and measure throughput and final taste scores.

name: Chisel
text:
Keep the Designs tab pure with an automated first-pass filter that rejects submissions failing basic taste rules (e.g., nudity, watermarks, extreme blur), then route the rest to a fast, lightweight human triage for final approval. This keeps the queue flowing while still enforcing quality—accepting the trade-off that a few borderline cases might slip through the filter.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s filter risks over-rejecting creative work that bends taste rules without breaking them—think edgy but intentional design. A better alternative: let the submitter self-grade against *clear, public* taste criteria before submission, then auto-approve if they pass, reserving human review for edge cases. Settle it by A/B testing both approaches with Marketing’s SLA data.
